solution:
**Data:** constant external pressure \( p = 1 \) atm \( = 1.013 \times 10^{5} \) Pa, \( V_{1} = 5 \) litre, \( V_{2} = 10 \) litre, heat absorbed \( Q = +400 \) J.

**Sign convention.** The first law is written \( \Delta U = Q - W \), where \( Q \) is the heat added TO the system and \( W \) is the work done BY the system. Heat absorbed is therefore positive, and work done by an expanding gas is positive.

**Work done by the gas.** The expansion is against a constant external pressure, so
\( \Delta V = (10 - 5) \) litre \( = 5 \) litre \( = 5 \times 10^{-3} \) m\( ^{3} \)
\( W = p \, \Delta V = (1.013 \times 10^{5}) \times (5 \times 10^{-3}) = 506.5 \) J

**Change in internal energy.**
\( \Delta U = Q - W = 400 - 506.5 = -106.5 \) J

The gas pushes out \( 506.5 \) J of work while drawing in only \( 400 \) J of heat, so the shortfall of \( 106.5 \) J comes out of its own internal energy. The internal energy therefore **decreases**, which is why the answer is negative.

(Taking the exact value \( 1 \) atm \( = 1.01325 \times 10^{5} \) Pa gives \( W = 506.6 \) J and \( \Delta U = -106.6 \) J -- the same answer to three significant figures.)

**Answer: \( \Delta U = -106.5 \) J, i.e. the internal energy of the gas decreases by about \( 106.5 \) J.**

[Textbook answer-key error: the printed key gives \(\Delta U = 21\) kJ, dropping the sign. The question asks for the CHANGE in internal energy, which here is a DECREASE. With the chapter's own convention \(\Delta U = Q - W\) (eq. 4.3, \(W\) the work done BY the system): the system releases heat, so \(Q = -130\) kJ, and work is done ON it, so \(W = -109\) kJ, giving \(\Delta U = -130 - (-109) = -21\) kJ. The sign does not depend on which convention is used — reading it as \(\Delta U = Q + W_{\text{on}} = -130 + 109\) returns the same \(-21\) kJ. Physically the system loses 130 kJ and gains 109 kJ, so 21 kJ leaves it.]

**Data:** heat released by the system \( = 130 \) kJ; work done ON the system \( = 109 \) kJ.

**Sign convention.** With the first law written \( \Delta U = Q - W \), \( Q \) is the heat added TO the system and \( W \) is the work done BY the system. Both quantities here are given in the opposite sense, so both are negative:
\( Q = -130 \) kJ (heat is released, not absorbed)
\( W = -109 \) kJ (work is done on the gas, not by it)

**Change in internal energy.**
\( \Delta U = Q - W = (-130) - (-109) = -130 + 109 = -21 \) kJ

**Check with the other form of the first law.** Writing it as \( \Delta U = Q + W_{\text{on}} \), where \( W_{\text{on}} \) is the work done on the system,
\( \Delta U = -130 + 109 = -21 \) kJ, the same result. The sign does not depend on which of the two standard conventions is used.

**Reading the sign physically:** the system loses \( 130 \) kJ as heat and gains only \( 109 \) kJ as work, so \( 21 \) kJ of energy leaves it on balance. Its internal energy must therefore fall.

**Answer: \( \Delta U = -21 \) kJ, i.e. the internal energy decreases by \( 21 \) kJ.**

[Textbook answer-key error: the printed key gives \(23^\circ\text{C}\); the correct cold-reservoir temperature is \(-23^\circ\text{C}\). Carnot efficiency uses ABSOLUTE temperature: \(T_H = 727^\circ\text{C} = 1000\) K, and \(\eta = 1 - T_C/T_H = 0.75\) gives \(T_C = 250\) K \(= -23^\circ\text{C}\). The key is self-refuting: \(+23^\circ\text{C} = 296\) K would make \(\eta = 1 - 296/1000 = 0.704\), not the 75% the question states.]

**Data:** efficiency of the Carnot cycle \( \eta = 75\% = 0.75 \); temperature of the hot reservoir \( T_{H} = 727\,^\circ\text{C} \).

**Convert to absolute temperature first.** The Carnot efficiency is defined in terms of thermodynamic (kelvin) temperatures, so a Celsius value must never be substituted directly:
\( T_{H} = 727 + 273 = 1000 \) K

**Relation.** For a Carnot cycle
\( \eta = 1 - \dfrac{T_{C}}{T_{H}} \)

**Substitute.**
\( 0.75 = 1 - \dfrac{T_{C}}{1000} \)
\( \dfrac{T_{C}}{1000} = 1 - 0.75 = 0.25 \)
\( T_{C} = 0.25 \times 1000 = 250 \) K

**Back to the Celsius scale.**
\( T_{C} = 250 - 273 = -23\,^\circ\text{C} \)

The cold reservoir must be well below the ice point: a Carnot engine can only reach an efficiency as high as \( 75\% \) between these limits if the sink is at \( 250 \) K, one quarter of the source temperature on the absolute scale.

**Answer: \( T_{C} = 250 \) K \( = -23\,^\circ\text{C} \).**

**Data:** Carnot refrigerator working between \( T_{C} = 250 \) K (the cold body, from which heat is extracted) and \( T_{H} = 300 \) K (the surroundings, to which heat is rejected). Both are already absolute temperatures.

**Relation.** A refrigerator is rated by its coefficient of performance, not by an efficiency. It is the heat extracted from the cold body per unit of work supplied, and for a Carnot refrigerator
\( \text{CoP} = \dfrac{Q_{C}}{W} = \dfrac{T_{C}}{T_{H} - T_{C}} \)

**Substitute.**
\( \text{CoP} = \dfrac{250}{300 - 250} = \dfrac{250}{50} = 5 \)

So for every \( 1 \) J of work supplied to the refrigerator, \( 5 \) J of heat are removed from the cold chamber (and \( 6 \) J are dumped into the surroundings).

Note that the engine formula \( \eta = 1 - T_{C}/T_{H} \) would give \( 1/6 \approx 0.167 \); that is the efficiency of a Carnot *engine* running between the same two reservoirs and is a different quantity from the coefficient of performance. Indeed \( \text{CoP} = (1 - \eta)/\eta = (5/6) \div (1/6) = 5 \), which is a useful cross-check.

**Answer: \( \text{CoP} = 5 \) (a pure number, it has no unit).**

**Data:** the process is isothermal; the gas does \( 2000 \) J of work on its environment, so the work done BY the system is \( W = +2000 \) J.

**Key idea.** The internal energy of an ideal gas depends only on its temperature. In an isothermal process the temperature is held constant, therefore
\( \Delta U = 0 \)

**First law.** With \( \Delta U = Q - W \), where \( Q \) is the heat added to the gas,
\( 0 = Q - 2000 \)
\( Q = 2000 \) J

Every joule of heat supplied is passed straight on as work done on the surroundings; none of it is stored as internal energy. This is the only kind of process in which the heat supplied and the work done are equal.

The sign is positive, so the heat is **added to** the gas (absorbed), consistent with a gas that is expanding while its temperature is held fixed.

**Answer: \( Q = 2000 \) J of heat is added to the gas.**

**Data:** the gas is ideal and monatomic, so \( \gamma = \dfrac{5}{3} \); the compression is adiabatic; \( T_{f} = 2 T_{i} \). Required: \( \dfrac{p_{f}}{p_{i}} \).

**Relation.** For a reversible adiabatic process \( pV^{\gamma} = \) constant. Eliminating \( V \) with the ideal gas equation \( pV = nRT \) gives the pressure-temperature form
\( T^{\gamma} p^{1-\gamma} = \) constant, i.e. \( \dfrac{p_{f}}{p_{i}} = \left( \dfrac{T_{f}}{T_{i}} \right)^{\frac{\gamma}{\gamma - 1}} \)

**Evaluate the exponent.**
\( \gamma - 1 = \dfrac{5}{3} - 1 = \dfrac{2}{3} \), so \( \dfrac{\gamma}{\gamma - 1} = \dfrac{5/3}{2/3} = \dfrac{5}{2} = 2.5 \)

**Substitute.**
\( \dfrac{p_{f}}{p_{i}} = 2^{5/2} = 4\sqrt{2} = 5.657 \)

**Independent check through the volume.** From \( T V^{\gamma - 1} = \) constant,
\( \dfrac{V_{f}}{V_{i}} = \left( \dfrac{T_{i}}{T_{f}} \right)^{\frac{1}{\gamma - 1}} = \left( \dfrac{1}{2} \right)^{3/2} = 0.3536 \)
and then from \( pV^{\gamma} = \) constant,
\( \dfrac{p_{f}}{p_{i}} = \left( \dfrac{V_{i}}{V_{f}} \right)^{\gamma} = (2.828)^{5/3} = 5.657 \), which agrees.

The ratio is greater than \( 1 \), as it must be: the gas is compressed, so its pressure rises.

**Answer: \( \dfrac{p_{f}}{p_{i}} = 2^{5/2} = 4\sqrt{2} \approx 5.66 \) (the final pressure is about \( 5.66 \) times the initial pressure).**

**Reading the graph.** The cycle is the closed loop drawn on the \( p \)-\( V \) plane. Its pressure axis is graduated in units of \( 10^{5} \) Pa and its volume axis in units of \( 10^{-3} \) m\( ^{3} \). The dashed guide lines show that the loop just touches
\( p = 11 \times 10^{5} \) Pa at the top and \( p = 1 \times 10^{5} \) Pa at the bottom,
\( V = 2 \times 10^{-3} \) m\( ^{3} \) on the left and \( V = 6 \times 10^{-3} \) m\( ^{3} \) on the right.

Although it is drawn as a circle on the page, the two axes carry different scales, so in \( (p, V) \) coordinates the loop is an **ellipse** centred at \( \left( 4 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{m}^{3},\ 6 \times 10^{5}\ \text{Pa} \right) \) with semi-axes
\( a = \dfrac{6 - 2}{2} \times 10^{-3} = 2 \times 10^{-3} \) m\( ^{3} \) along \( V \)
\( b = \dfrac{11 - 1}{2} \times 10^{5} = 5 \times 10^{5} \) Pa along \( p \)

**Key idea.** The work done in one complete cycle is the area enclosed by the loop on the \( p \)-\( V \) diagram, \( W = \oint p \, dV \). For an ellipse that area is \( \pi a b \).

**Work in one cycle.**
\( W_{1} = \pi a b = \pi \times (2 \times 10^{-3}) \times (5 \times 10^{5}) = \pi \times 10^{3} = 3.142 \times 10^{3} \) J

**Work in \( 25 \) cycles.**
\( W = 25 \times 3.142 \times 10^{3} = 7.855 \times 10^{4} \) J

(Using \( \pi = 3.1416 \) gives \( 7.854 \times 10^{4} \) J; the two agree to three significant figures.)

The unit checks out: pressure \( \times \) volume is Pa \( \times \) m\( ^{3} \) \( = \) N m\( ^{-2} \times \) m\( ^{3} = \) N m \( = \) J.

**Answer: \( W \approx 7.86 \times 10^{4} \) J \( \left( 7.855 \times 10^{4}\ \text{J} \right) \) in \( 25 \) cycles, i.e. about \( 3.14 \times 10^{3} \) J per cycle. If the loop is traced clockwise this is the work done by the gas on its surroundings; traced anticlockwise, the same amount of work is done on the gas.**

**Reading the given \( V \)-\( T \) diagram.** The cycle runs \( a \rightarrow b \rightarrow c \rightarrow d \rightarrow a \). The states \( a \) and \( d \) lie on the same vertical line, so they are at the same temperature \( T_{1} \); the states \( b \) and \( c \) lie on a second vertical line at a higher temperature \( T_{2} \). Reading the volumes off the vertical axis gives the order
\( V_{d} < V_{c} < V_{a} < V_{b} \)

So the four steps are:
- \( a \rightarrow b \): both \( V \) and \( T \) increase (a general process, neither isothermal nor isochoric)
- \( b \rightarrow c \): a vertical line at \( T_{2} \), so \( T \) is constant while \( V \) decreases -- an **isothermal compression**
- \( c \rightarrow d \): both \( V \) and \( T \) decrease
- \( d \rightarrow a \): a vertical line at \( T_{1} \), so \( T \) is constant while \( V \) increases -- an **isothermal expansion**

**Getting the pressures.** For the ideal gas, \( pV = nRT \), so \( p = \dfrac{nRT}{V} \). Applying this to the four states read off the graph:
\( p_{a} \propto \dfrac{T_{1}}{V_{a}} \), \( p_{b} \propto \dfrac{T_{2}}{V_{b}} \), \( p_{c} \propto \dfrac{T_{2}}{V_{c}} \), \( p_{d} \propto \dfrac{T_{1}}{V_{d}} \)

Because \( V_{d} \) is the smallest volume and \( V_{b} \) the largest, and \( T_{2} > T_{1} \), the pressures come out in the order
\( p_{a} < p_{b} < p_{d} < p_{c} \)

**The \( p \)-\( V \) diagram.** Plot \( p \) vertically against \( V \) horizontally and mark the four states using the two orders above -- \( a \) at the bottom (lowest pressure, middling volume), \( b \) to its right (largest volume, slightly higher pressure), \( c \) at the top (highest pressure, small volume) and \( d \) on the left (smallest volume, pressure between \( p_{b} \) and \( p_{c} \)). Then join them:
- \( b \rightarrow c \) and \( d \rightarrow a \) are isotherms, so each is drawn as a **rectangular hyperbola** \( pV = \) constant, the \( b \rightarrow c \) arc lying on the hotter (outer) isotherm
- \( a \rightarrow b \) and \( c \rightarrow d \) are the two general steps and are drawn as the gentler curves closing the loop

The result is a curved four-sided loop, traversed \( a \rightarrow b \rightarrow c \rightarrow d \rightarrow a \), which is the **anticlockwise** sense on the \( p \)-\( V \) plane.

**The \( p \)-\( T \) diagram.** Plot \( p \) vertically against \( T \) horizontally. States \( a \) and \( d \) sit on the vertical line \( T = T_{1} \) and states \( b \) and \( c \) on the vertical line \( T = T_{2} \), with the same pressure order \( p_{a} < p_{b} < p_{d} < p_{c} \). Hence:
- \( a \rightarrow b \): a line sloping **up to the right** (both \( p \) and \( T \) increase)
- \( b \rightarrow c \): a **vertical line upwards** at \( T = T_{2} \) -- the isothermal compression raises the pressure at constant temperature
- \( c \rightarrow d \): a line sloping **down to the left** (both \( p \) and \( T \) decrease)
- \( d \rightarrow a \): a **vertical line downwards** at \( T = T_{1} \) -- the isothermal expansion lowers the pressure at constant temperature

The \( p \)-\( T \) diagram is therefore a slanted quadrilateral with two vertical sides, one at \( T_{1} \) and one at \( T_{2} \).

**Answer: on the \( p \)-\( V \) plane the cycle is a curved loop whose \( b \rightarrow c \) and \( d \rightarrow a \) sides are isotherms (rectangular hyperbolae), with the states in the order \( p_{a} < p_{b} < p_{d} < p_{c} \) and \( V_{d} < V_{c} < V_{a} < V_{b} \); on the \( p \)-\( T \) plane it is a slanted quadrilateral whose \( b \rightarrow c \) and \( d \rightarrow a \) sides are vertical lines at \( T_{2} \) and \( T_{1} \) respectively.**

[Textbook answer-key error: the printed key gives \(W_{AB} = 2.4 \times 10^{6}\) J and \(W_{CD} = -8 \times 10^{5}\) J, each \(10^{3}\) too large. The figure's volume axis is labelled \(V(\text{L})\) — litres — so \(\Delta V = 4\ \text{L} = 4 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{m}^3\), giving \(W_{AB} = (6 \times 10^{5})(4 \times 10^{-3}) = 2.4 \times 10^{3}\) J and \(W_{CD} = (2 \times 10^{5})(-4 \times 10^{-3}) = -8 \times 10^{2}\) J. The printed values are what the litre-to-\(\text{m}^3\) conversion being omitted produces. The book handles the same conversion correctly in Q.10 on this very page, whose axis reads \(V(10^{-3}\text{m}^3)\). The key's remaining claims are right: \(W_{BC} = W_{DA} = 0\), those legs being at constant volume.]

**Reading the graph.** The pressure axis is graduated in units of \( 10^{5} \) Pa and the volume axis is marked \( V(\text{L}) \), i.e. in litres, with \( 1 \) litre \( = 10^{-3} \) m\( ^{3} \). The four states are
\( A = \left( 2\ \text{L},\ 6 \times 10^{5}\ \text{Pa} \right) \), \( B = \left( 6\ \text{L},\ 6 \times 10^{5}\ \text{Pa} \right) \), \( C = \left( 6\ \text{L},\ 2 \times 10^{5}\ \text{Pa} \right) \), \( D = \left( 2\ \text{L},\ 2 \times 10^{5}\ \text{Pa} \right) \)
and the arrows run \( A \rightarrow B \rightarrow C \rightarrow D \rightarrow A \).

**Relations.** Work done by the gas is \( W = \int p \, dV \). For a path at constant pressure this is \( W = p \, \Delta V \); for a path at constant volume \( \Delta V = 0 \), so \( W = 0 \) whatever the pressure does.

**Path \( A \rightarrow B \)** -- horizontal, so isobaric at \( p = 6 \times 10^{5} \) Pa, with \( \Delta V = (6 - 2)\ \text{L} = 4 \times 10^{-3} \) m\( ^{3} \):
\( W_{AB} = (6 \times 10^{5}) \times (4 \times 10^{-3}) = 2.4 \times 10^{3} \) J
Positive, because the gas expands and does work on the surroundings.

**Path \( B \rightarrow C \)** -- vertical, so isochoric at \( V = 6 \) L. \( \Delta V = 0 \), hence
\( W_{BC} = 0 \)

**Path \( C \rightarrow D \)** -- horizontal, so isobaric at \( p = 2 \times 10^{5} \) Pa, with \( \Delta V = (2 - 6)\ \text{L} = -4 \times 10^{-3} \) m\( ^{3} \):
\( W_{CD} = (2 \times 10^{5}) \times (-4 \times 10^{-3}) = -8 \times 10^{2} \) J
Negative, because the gas is compressed and work is done on it.

**Path \( D \rightarrow A \)** -- vertical, so isochoric at \( V = 2 \) L. \( \Delta V = 0 \), hence
\( W_{DA} = 0 \)

**Net work in the complete cycle.**
\( W_{\text{net}} = 2.4 \times 10^{3} + 0 - 8 \times 10^{2} + 0 = 1.6 \times 10^{3} \) J
This equals the area of the enclosed rectangle, \( \left( 6 - 2 \right) \times 10^{5}\ \text{Pa} \times \left( 6 - 2 \right) \times 10^{-3}\ \text{m}^{3} = 1.6 \times 10^{3} \) J, which is a useful check. It is positive because the loop is traced clockwise, so the gas does net work on its surroundings.

**Answer: \( W_{AB} = 2.4 \times 10^{3} \) J, \( W_{BC} = 0 \), \( W_{CD} = -8 \times 10^{2} \) J, \( W_{DA} = 0 \); the two vertical paths do no work because the volume does not change, and the net work per cycle is \( 1.6 \times 10^{3} \) J.**
